architectural_implications.after: A harness component owns context assembly, loop control, environments, and extension points, with the model as a replaceable dependency.
architectural_implications.before: Prompt strings, retrieval calls, and tool loops scattered through application code with the model treated as the architecture.
architectural_implications.consequence: Enables model switching and middleware-based extension without rewriting domain logic, but requires investing in context plumbing up front.
architectural_implications.observation: The harness becomes an explicit, named layer boundary between model and context rather than implicit glue code inside an application.

architectural_implications.after: Shared open-source eval runners where custom and off-the-shelf harnesses are measured on the same tasks.
architectural_implications.before: Per-team, bespoke eval scripts that are not comparable across harnesses or models.
architectural_implications.consequence: Harness choices become empirically comparable and regressions detectable, but pushes teams toward standard task suites that may not reflect private domain quality.
architectural_implications.observation: Evaluation becomes transportable infrastructure via a standard runner (Harbor), making harness/model comparisons a routine benchmark operation.

architectural_implications.after: Inspecting full LLM inputs, outputs, and message trajectories to locate context defects.
architectural_implications.before: Tuning prompts and upgrading models in response to bad answers.
architectural_implications.consequence: Observability tooling (trace views with tool calls, latencies, token costs) becomes a first-class runtime dependency rather than a monitoring afterthought.
architectural_implications.observation: Debugging interfaces shift from model-output inspection toward trajectory-level context inspection.

architectural_implications.after: Systems mine traces, group failures into an issue board, and propose prompt or harness modifications for review.
architectural_implications.before: Humans read traces, cluster failures by hand, and write fixes.
architectural_implications.consequence: Human effort concentrates on validating and reviewing proposed fixes, introducing a new review bottleneck and a need to measure auto-proposed changes.
architectural_implications.observation: The improvement loop is closed by automation that reads traces and emits proposed changes to prompts and harnesses.

article_ideas.angle: Reframe agent engineering from model choice to context-getting: the harness is the layer that owns fixed versus dynamic context, environments, loop control, and extension points.

article_ideas.based_on: A harness gets the model the right context at the right time
article_ideas.thesis: Agent quality is decided in context assembly and orchestration, not model selection; teams that treat the model as the architecture will keep buying upgrades to fix defects that live upstream of the model.
article_ideas.title: The Harness Is the Product — The Model Is a Swappable Dependency

article_ideas.angle: Walk the lock-in failure mode: swapping an API endpoint while episodic, semantic, and procedural memory remain framework internals means the institutional knowledge stays with the vendor.

article_ideas.based_on: To own your intelligence, you have to own all three parts.

article_ideas.angle: Give the decision rule with its missing measurement: define in-distribution versus out-of-distribution signals, name the middleware ceiling symptoms, and price the late migration.
article_ideas.audience: Staff engineers and agent framework maintainers
article_ideas.based_on: Customizing harnesses can be done via middleware (hooks and plugins) or custom cognitive architectures
article_ideas.thesis: Extension points are the correct default and a full architectural fork should be triggered by a measured shift in task distribution, not by ambition, so the engineering question is the crossover criterion rather than the aesthetic of a custom loop.
article_ideas.title: Middleware Until It Breaks: A Migration Rule for Agent Architecture

article_ideas.angle: Argue the trace store is the durable, reusable artifact and eval runners plus issue boards are the machinery that turns it into hill-climbing progress.
article_ideas.audience: Applied AI engineers and MLOps practitioners
article_ideas.based_on: A continuous learning loop acts as a hill-climbing machine to compound AI investment value.

Production traces are the raw input that the flywheel mines and curates into experiments, making tracing a prerequisite for continuous improvement.
Portability of the model layer depends on owning the context substrate; switching models without owned context forfeits institutional memory.
Public benchmarks measure general harness quality while private evals define organization-specific quality and catch regressions.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Harrison Chase
  • Channel: Sequoia Capital
  • Main topic: Agent harnesses, evals, observability, and continuous improvement loops for LLM agents
  • Purpose: To provide technical guidance on building, evaluating, and improving agent harnesses and continuous learning systems for AI applications. Harrison Chase, co-founder and CEO of LangChain, discusses the core anatomy of LLM agents—breaking them down into models, context, and harnesses. He covers when to build custom agent harnesses versus using off-the-shelf options, the importance of evals and observability (benchmarking with tools like Harbor), and the creation of a continuous learning data flywheel using tools like LangSmith Engine.

Topic Map

Parts of an Agent

  • Explanation: An agent consists of three core components: a model, context, and a harness that orchestrates them.
  • Key claims:
    • To own your intelligence, you must own all three parts: model, context, and harness.
    • Model ownership involves open weights and the ability to switch models.
    • Context ownership includes episodic, semantic, and procedural memory.
  • Examples:
    • Switching models to avoid lock-in and use the best model available.
    • Using RAG and chat history as semantic and episodic context.
  • Terminology:
    • harness
    • model
    • context
    • open weights
    • RAG
  • Why it matters: Understanding the components of an agent is essential for owning and customizing AI intelligence effectively.

How to Own Your Harness

  • Explanation: A harness gets the model the right context at the right time for a given task, orchestrating fixed and dynamic context.
  • Key claims:
    • Agents need environments, data connections, long-run context management, parallelization, human-in-the-loop, and self-improvement.
    • The base agent loop is an LLM calling tools in a loop until a task completes.
    • Customizing harnesses can be done via middleware (hooks and plugins) or custom cognitive architectures.
  • Examples:
    • LangChain as a base minimal harness vs. DeepAgents as a customizable harness.
    • Adding summarization, sandbox environments, and sub-agents as middleware.
  • Terminology:
    • middleware
    • hooks
    • plugins
    • sandboxes
    • sub-agents
    • context offloading
  • Why it matters: Harness engineering allows developers to adapt general models into specialized, reliable agents for domain-specific tasks.

Evals and Observability

  • Explanation: Every mission-critical agent needs benchmarks to define what 'good' looks like and catch regressions.
  • Key claims:
    • Private evals define quality inside an organization.
    • Harbor is becoming an industry-standard open source eval runner.
    • Observability into LLM inputs, outputs, and message trajectories is critical for debugging agent failures.
  • Examples:
    • Frontier-bench and Terminal-bench as coding agent benchmarks.
    • LangSmith trace views showing tool calls, latencies, and token costs.
  • Terminology:
    • evals
    • observability
    • Harbor
    • frontier-bench
    • trajectories
    • traces
  • Why it matters: Without proper evals and observability, debugging agents and preventing regressions is nearly impossible.

Data Flywheel and Continuous Improvement

  • Explanation: Building a continuous learning loop requires collecting traces, mining data, curating evals, and running experiments.
  • Key claims:
    • A continuous learning loop acts as a hill-climbing machine to compound AI investment value.
    • Feedback is crucial for the flywheel, coming from UX design and synthetic feedback (online evals).
    • LangSmith Engine automates trace data analysis to create issue boards and suggest prompt or harness fixes.
  • Examples:
    • Using fine-tuned SLMs as judges to reduce evaluation costs.
    • LangSmith Engine automatically grouping agent failure traces and proposing prompt modifications.
  • Terminology:
    • data flywheel
    • synthetic feedback
    • online evals
    • SLM judges
    • LangSmith Engine
    • issue board
  • Why it matters: Automating the feedback and iteration loop enables agents to improve continuously over time with minimal manual overhead.

Key Points

Anatomy of an Agent

  • Explanation: Agents are composed of three parts: a model, context, and a harness.
  • Evidence: Diagrams showing harness wrapping model and context.
  • Practical implication: Developers should control all three layers to avoid vendor lock-in and maximize agent performance.

When to Build vs. Use Off-the-Shelf Harnesses

  • Explanation: Off-the-shelf harnesses work well for in-distribution tasks, while custom harnesses are needed for out-of-distribution tasks.
  • Evidence: Discussion of Codex/Claude Code vs. specialized domain harnesses like legal AI.
  • Practical implication: Start with general off-the-shelf harnesses and customize or build proprietary ones as domain specificity increases.

The Importance of Observability

  • Explanation: Most agent failures stem from poor context fed to the LLM rather than model incompetence.
  • Evidence: Analysis of LLM call errors and trace trajectories.
  • Practical implication: Implement detailed trace logging and trajectory inspection to effectively debug agent behaviors.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Recipe for Continuously Improving Agents

  • How it works: A four-step iterative process to upgrade agent performance using production data.
  • Components:
    • Build a v1 agent and start running it
    • Collect lots of traces
    • Curate the trace data via data mining
    • Run experiments on your data
  • When to use: When deploying production LLM agents that need to improve over time based on real usage.

Examples & Case Studies

Comparing Codex, Claude Code, and DeepAgents on coding benchmarks using Harbor.

  • Illustrates: How different agent harnesses and models perform across standardized tasks.
  • Lesson: Benchmarking allows developers to quantitatively evaluate trade-offs between different models and harness architectures.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Define private evals and benchmarks for your critical agents.
    • Ensure robust tracing and observability are set up from day one.
    • Start with simple general harnesses before building custom cognitive architectures.
  • Strategic:
    • Own your model, context, and harness to retain organizational memory and institutional knowledge.
    • Build a data flywheel using trace mining and automated feedback loops.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • When does an out-of-distribution task justify building a fully custom cognitive architecture?
    • How can synthetic evaluation costs be minimized at scale?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Harbor is becoming an industry-standard open source eval runner. (industry trend)
  • Most agent errors are caused by poor context rather than poor model capability. (technical assertion)

Notable Quotes

"To own your intelligence, you have to own all three parts." "Create your private evals, because evals define what good looks like inside the organization."

Compressed Summary

  • Agents consist of models, context, and harnesses.
  • Harness engineering involves middleware and custom cognitive architectures.
  • Evals and benchmarking via tools like Harbor catch regressions.
  • Observability into trace trajectories is critical for debugging agent failures.
  • LangSmith Engine powers a data flywheel for continuous agent improvement.
  • Keywords: agent harness, evals, observability, traces, data flywheel
  • Core insight: Owning your agent intelligence requires controlling models, context, and harnesses while powering continuous improvement through robust evals, observability, and data flywheels.

## Key Points
### Anatomy of an Agent
- **Explanation**: Agents are composed of three parts: a model, context, and a harness.
- **Evidence**: Diagrams showing harness wrapping model and context.
- **Practical implication**: Developers should control all three layers to avoid vendor lock-in and maximize agent performance.
### When to Build vs. Use Off-the-Shelf Harnesses
- **Explanation**: Off-the-shelf harnesses work well for in-distribution tasks, while custom harnesses are needed for out-of-distribution tasks.
- **Evidence**: Discussion of Codex/Claude Code vs. specialized domain harnesses like legal AI.
- **Practical implication**: Start with general off-the-shelf harnesses and customize or build proprietary ones as domain specificity increases.
### The Importance of Observability
- **Explanation**: Most agent failures stem from poor context fed to the LLM rather than model incompetence.
- **Evidence**: Analysis of LLM call errors and trace trajectories.
- **Practical implication**: Implement detailed trace logging and trajectory inspection to effectively debug agent behaviors.
